articles.title_orig: Duchess of Sussex was told of ‘disturbing allegations’ against her father in 2018
articles.title_zh: Duchess of Sussex was told of ‘disturbing allegations’ against her father in 2018
articles.content_orig:
Meghan reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police
The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.
Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
Sources said although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2018, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the Rasp unit within the Met police.
It is understood the Met has not previously investigated Markle Sr, nor is it currently doing so. The force said it was making internal inquiries regarding officers from Rasp being involved in the passing on of a letter.
A Met spokesperson said: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s royalty and specialist protection command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.”
Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
The FBI said in a statement: “The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”
The undersecretary for the Philippines’ justice department, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC the matter was being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu.
The interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, separately told the BBC that national police had secured Markle Sr’s computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Remulla said it would take “one week to get the forensic [results]”.
Meghan’s father has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”
Meghan’s half-sister Samantha Markle has defended their father, accusing her brother Markle Jr of “making up lies” to make money.
She told the Mail: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
She alleged her brother made the allegations days after their father cut off his funds, “and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to make money from the media”.
She alleged the computers were not in her father’s possession for two years and he could have been set up. “That leaves a lot of room for tampering,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Ebola: Kenya records second death as 65-year-old woman succumbs
articles.title_zh: Ebola: Kenya records second death as 65-year-old woman succumbs
articles.content_orig:
The 65-year-old woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and died while receiving care at an infectious disease unit
Kenya’s health ministry announced the country’s second Ebola death on Friday, saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The ministry said medical personnel “did everything possible to save her life”, but she died Friday evening.
Her family was notified, and the ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.

articles.title_orig: Over 4 million tubes of toothpaste have been recalled, including kids brands — here’s what you need to know
articles.title_zh: Over 4 million tubes of toothpaste have been recalled, including kids brands — here’s what you need to know
articles.content_orig:
NBC Selected independently determines what we cover and recommend. When you click on or buy through our links, we earn a commission. Learn more .
More than 4.3 million tubes of fluoride toothpaste — many of them kid-themed , in flavors like bubble gum, strawberry and watermelon — have been voluntarily recalled nationwide after the Food and Drug Administration flagged manufacturing problems at the facility that made them.
The recall covers several brands sold under licensed character names, along with a handful of lesser-known labels, and includes tubes with expiration dates stretching into mid-2028, meaning some of the affected toothpaste could be sitting in your medicine cabinet right now.
No illnesses or injuries have been reported. Still, the FDA says families should check lot numbers and expiration dates to see whether their toothpaste is part of the recall. Below, I break down exactly which products are affected, how to tell if you have one and what to do next.
The FDA announced the recall of more than 4.3 million tubes of fluoride toothpaste distributed nationwide because of current good manufacturing practice deviations. Those are federal standards meant to ensure products are made consistently and safely, so a deviation means the manufacturing process didn’t meet requirements, not necessarily that the toothpaste itself is harmful.
The voluntary recall was initiated on September 10 by Pritam International Private Limited, an India-based manufacturer, and the FDA classified it as Class II recall on October 19. A Class II recall is for products that could cause temporary or medically reversible health problems, where the chance of serious harm is considered unlikely. The FDA notice did not report any illnesses or injuries linked to the recalled toothpaste.
Many of the affected tubes were marketed to kids. The recalled products include toothpaste sold under the Brush Buddies, Crayola, Hot Wheels and My Little Pony brands, in flavors such as bubble gum, strawberry, watermelon, peppermint, sweet mint and cool mint. They were distributed by Ashtel Studios Inc. of Ontario, California, and come in 3.5-ounce and 4-ounce tubes, plus a two-pack of 3.5-ounce tubes.
Affected products carry expiration dates from November 2026 through June 2028, and consumers should check the lot numbers and expiration dates on the FDA’s recall notice to see whether theirs is included.
The FDA’s recall notice doesn’t include specific instructions for consumers, and neither the manufacturer nor the distributor has issued public guidance on returns or refunds. Until they do, the safest move is to stop using the toothpaste immediately and toss it out. Start by checking the brand, lot number and expiration date on your tube against the FDA’s recall notice; if it matches, discard it and switch to a different fluoride toothpaste so your family’s brushing routine isn’t interrupted.
Hang on to your receipt or take a photo of the packaging before tossing it, in case a refund process is announced later. No illnesses or injuries have been reported, but if you or your child used the product and have any concerns, you should contact your dentist or doctor immediately.
The below toothpastes were not recalled and have at least a four-star average rating from thousands of customers.
My kids absolutely love this toothpaste — in fact, it is the only one they will use. The fruity flavor makes brushing less of a chore, while fluoride fights cavities and calcium and silica gently clean teeth. It’s approved by the American Dental Association (ADA), free of artificial colors, flavors, and preservatives, and suitable for children ages 2 and up.
This toothpaste’s bright blue, sparkly color will delight kids. Plus, the fluoride formula fights cavities while staying gentle on enamel, and it carries the ADA Seal of Acceptance . It is suitable for children ages 2 and up, with adult supervision.
If you can’t decide on which hello kids’ flavor your little one will love, grab this variety pack that lets them sample all three and pick a favorite. Each toothpaste comes in a brightly colored tube with an easy flip cap that sits flat when closed, so it stands neatly on the bathroom counter.
If you had one of the adult toothpastes in the recall, Crest Pro-Health Advanced is a reliable replacement from a brand you already know. It’s an antibacterial fluoride toothpaste that fights plaque bacteria and supports healthy gums. It also helps whiten teeth and strengthen enamel.

articles.title_orig: Dow tumbles more than 600 points as oil prices rise and market sell-off hits most sectors
articles.title_zh: Dow tumbles more than 600 points as oil prices rise and market sell-off hits most sectors
articles.content_orig:
The FTSE 100 has slumped after the UK’s borrowing costs climbed to their highest level since 1998.
Britain’s flagship stock index declined as much as 2pc on Thursday in its worst performance since May. Banks pushed the stock index lower as the financial sector was rocked by the bond sell-off.
Yields on 30-year gilts, which determine the interest the Treasury pays to borrow over that period, broke above 6pc for the first time in 28 years.
It marked the first time that any G7 nation has faced an interest rate of more than 6pc on its debt since Italy during the eurozone debt crisis in 2012.
Traders fear that a prolonged Iran war energy price shock will limit economic growth and force central banks to raise interest rates.
The Bank of England is expected to increase borrowing costs in November ahead of a predicted surge in energy bills over winter. Markets are betting that UK interest rates will hit 4.75pc by July next year.
Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, ordered Iranian negotiators to leave the US overnight after the two sides failed to make progress on an end to the conflict.
Tensions in the Middle East were raised further by an attempted hijacking of a plane carrying Israeli passengers to Tel Aviv on Wednesday.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said: “US-Iran talks remained in stalemate. Reports of a possible hijacking of a Dubai to Tel Aviv flight brought back concerns over increasing risk of terrorism.”
The 10-year US Treasury bond yield – a benchmark for the cost of government borrowing around the world – jumped to 5.33pc, a level it last reached in 2002.
Read the latest updates below.
Thank you for following our live updates of today’s bond sell-off and the slump in the stock markets.
Taking a look at the FTSE 100, the index is down 1.68pc for the day as bank stocks pull lower.
The yield on 30-year gilts has fallen back slightly to 5.93pc after topping 6pc earlier, the highest level since 1998.
You can stay up to date with all the latest business news here.
UK bank stocks dropped sharply on Thursday, as 30-year gilts reached their highest levels since 1998.
Major lenders saw heavy losses, as NatWest fell 5.2pc, Lloyds dropped 4.4pc, and HSBC lost 4.3pc.
Barclays also slid nearly 4pc, as the FTSE 350 pulled lower in the afternoon session to 4.1pc.
The sell-off intensified following reports that top bank executives were summoned to meet John Healey ahead of the Budget, fuelling speculation about potential new taxes on the sector.
Earlier this week, Revolut was amongst a group of banks urging the chancellor to rules out tax rises on the sector.
Accenture shares have surged by 24pc after it beat forecasts, posting an 8pc rise in profits.
The consultancy, which employs 800,000 staff, has seen its stock slump sharply over the past few years over concern about the impacts of AI on its business.
However, Julie Sweet, its CEO, told a conference call that Accenture was boosted by demand for advice on AI and that the tech was making it more efficient.
Accenture is also investing in AI safety, in expectation that there will be a big growth in the sector, Ms Sweet said.
The Bank of England must raise interest rates to “maintain credibility” in the battle against inflation, a top policymaker has warned.
Catherine Mann, a member of the Monetary Policy Committee, said that at a time of rising inflation risks and the volatile war in Iran, it is important the Bank sets out its intentions clearly.
“Given rising upside risks to inflation, a risk management strategy to monetary policy is appropriate.
“When there is uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects, raising Bank Rate to commit to the inflation target can help ensure a sustainable return of inflation to the 2pc target, with smaller losses to economic activity,” she said.
“With the ‘sporadic continuance’ of the conflict in the Middle East, uncertainty around the outlook for the economy and inflation risks have remained elevated. Uncertainty about the MPC reaction function should not compound the problem.”
Inflation has so far risen to 3.1pc and is expected to rise above 4pc early next year.
Diesel prices are at a record high of around £2 per litre, while household energy bills are projected to rise by a further 16pc in January.
In turn this raises the danger of inflation spreading through more of the economy.
Ms Mann backed an increase in the Bank’s base rate from 3.75pc to 4pc in the past two MPC meetings, but was outvoted by the majority of the nine-strong panel.
“At some point, we need to follow through with Bank Rate rises – to maintain credibility, and to avoid policy expectations repricing downwards and inflation expectations repricing further upwards,” she said.
John Healey will meet with the chief executives of Britain’s banks next Tuesday ahead of his upcoming Budget.
Bosses from HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest, Santander UK, and Nationwide are amongst those summoned for talks with the chancellor, according to Sky News.
The meeting comes amidst growing industry anxiety over a potential bank tax raid in October.
The gathering will follow Mr Healey’s recent address at the Labour Party conference, where he pledged to work “in partnership with business and the unions”.
Unions have called on the chancellor to raise billions from the banks to help fund public services, given recent profits made by the sector.
The rally on Wall Street has been short lived after a spike in oil prices.
US stocks turned lower after the price of Brent crude climbed 3pc to nearly $101 a barrel, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.4pc.
The FTSE 100 was last down 1.5pc, while the Cac 40 in France fell 1.2pc.
The US stock market rallied at the open despite the pressure on bond markets.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5pc to 51,139.14 and the S&P 500 climbed 0.3pc to 7,674.66 even after the US 10-year Treasury bond yield hit its highest level since 2002.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite jumped 0.5pc to 26,999.09 after strong results from Micron boosted chip companies.
Opposition parties have questioned the Prime Minister’s handle on the recent rise in government borrowing costs.
Alex Burghart, the Tory deputy leader, told BBC Radio Kent: “We cannot afford to live like this.
“I was very worried to listen to Andy Burnham’s speech in Liverpool, where he had no plans to control government spending at all, and it’s like he’s not sort of looking at the financial markets in any way.”
Reform leader Nigel Farage said the Prime Minister “is not facing up to the reality that he can’t solve this crisis”.
The party’s economic spokesman Robert Jenrick suggested Mr Burnham would fail to curb borrowing costs with “unfunded promises on a National Care Service, a ballooning benefits bill and more delays for Heathrow”.
With the yield on 30-year US government debt at its highest since 2002, an obvious question to ask is why the stock market is so relaxed.
The cost of borrowing is back where it was before the financial crisis, bonds offer investors a viable alternative source of income again and the present-day value of future earnings is being squeezed. Why then are shares close to their all-time high ?
The obvious answer is that earnings continue to rise. We have had quarter after quarter of robust profits growth. Maybe that is reason enough. But even a cursory glance at history suggests that soaring bond yields can be the trigger for a stock market correction. The question remains: how high is too high for bond yields?
The global bond rout has abated in afternoon trading.
The yield on 10-year UK gilts sits 5.4pc, having risen as high as 5.5pc earlier, while the 30-year yield has eased back to 5.93pc, from as high as 6.02pc earlier.
France’s 10-year yield earlier closed in on the symbolic 5pc amid concerns over its unsustainable public finances. It touched 4.96pc earlier, its highest level since 2002, but has fallen back to 4.81pc.

articles.title_orig: Report: Apple gains ground in China as smartphone shipments hit 14-year low in Q3
articles.title_zh: Report: Apple gains ground in China as smartphone shipments hit 14-year low in Q3
articles.content_orig:
Rising memory prices continue to weigh on the global smartphone market, with shipments in China alone falling 10% year over year in Q3. Here are the details.
A few days ago, IDC reported that smartphone shipments in China fell 15.4% year over year in Q3 2026, with Apple increasing its share of that total to 17.8% despite a 4.3% decline in iPhone shipments.
The report echoed the broader global trend, with IDC estimating that worldwide smartphone shipments fell a record 22% year over year during the quarter, while Apple recorded the smallest decline among the top five manufacturers, at just 4%.
Now, a new report from Counterpoint Research paints a similar picture of China’s smartphone market in Q3, although its estimates differ somewhat from IDC’s.
According to the report, smartphone shipments in China hit a 14-year low during Q3 2026, with a 10% decline year over year.
Apple, on the other hand, accounted for 19.5% of smartphone shipments in China during the period, a 4.8-percentage-point increase year over year. The company was second only to Huawei, which held a 21.3% share, up 5.3 percentage points from a year earlier.
In fact, these were the only two among the top six brands to gain shipment share year over year, with vivo down 2.8 percentage points to 15.2%, OPPO down 1.3 points to 15.1%, Xiaomi down 1.6 points to 13.5%, HONOR down 2.2 points to 12.7%, and other manufacturers collectively down 2 points to 2.8%.
Notably, Apple went from sixth to second place in overall shipments, which Counterpoint attributes in part to the strong launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series:
Apple ranked second with a 19.5% market share in Q3. The iPhone 18 Pro series saw a strong launch in China, with sales in the first three weeks up 23.5% YoY compared with the iPhone 17 Pro series. The delayed launch of the base iPhone 18 may have encouraged some consumers to trade up to the Pro models, supporting their early sales momentum.
Looking ahead, Counterpoint noted that rising smartphone prices are leading consumers to delay upgrades, wait for promotional periods, or turn to refurbished devices, potentially putting further pressure on demand in Q4.
To check out Counterpoint Research’s full report, follow this link .

He began covering Apple news in Brazilian media in 2012 and later broadened his focus to the wider tech industry, hosting a daily podcast for seven years.

articles.title_orig: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
articles.title_zh: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.
At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack.
In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists".
Jordan's King Abdullah II, said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties".
Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.
Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.
Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows.
Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee.
Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active".
"People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said.
"Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church."
He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went".
Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started.
"I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic."
A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer.
"The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening.
"People started screaming.
The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards".
Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan".
There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed.
Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot.
Security measures were also tightened ahead of the visit by King Abdullah II to check on the injured.
The atmosphere around the hospital remained tense as the sound of crying and shouting was heard as families mourned their loved ones.
Many people appear shocked, frightened and angry. Some expressed frustration at what they described as "a failure to take a tougher approach towards terrorists".
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in the country, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the past.
Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.
Additional reporting by Majdi Gousous, BBC Arabic.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
articles.content_orig:
There were some big moves in telecommunications stocks on Friday. On one hand, shares of cell tower owners Crown Castle ( CCI +9.06% ) and American Tower ( AMT +4.08% ) soared, with shares up by about 9% and 4%, respectively, as of midday. On the other hand, the three largest wireless carriers plunged, with Verizon ( VZ -1.20% ) , AT&T ( T -7.96% ) , and T-Mobile ( TMUS -7.71% ) all deep in the red.
Both moves are due to one company, SpaceX ( SPCX +1.89% ) . On Thursday evening, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks to secure at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States as it aims to become the fourth nationwide wireless carrier. For context, 80,000 sites would represent about half of all the purpose-built cell towers in the U.S., so it would be a pretty big move.
Image source: Getty Images.
This is the second time in October that SpaceX has sent shockwaves through the telecom industry. First, on Oct. 9, SpaceX agreed to buy $8 billion in low-frequency wireless spectrum, and telecom stocks plunged. So, will SpaceX truly boost the tower companies and cost the telecom leaders money?
First, a little context on how the cell tower business works. The owner builds a tower and then rents space on it to wireless carriers, typically under long-term leases. Next time you drive by a cell tower, take a look at the top. You'll probably see several rings of transmission equipment, and each of those represents a tenant. Since the tower is already standing, adding tenants produces extra revenue with very little additional cost.
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/23/26
Ever since Sprint was acquired by T-Mobile, the tower industry has essentially had three wireless customers . The majority of Crown Castle's rent comes from AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. A well-capitalized fourth player would mean more tenants per tower.
This is also a notable expansion of SpaceX's plans. Although the company has made its telecom network ambitions known for some time, as recently as August, management described its network as small cells mounted on rooftops (not traditional towers). But without getting too technical, the low-band spectrum it bought makes large towers far more useful, so it makes sense to add them to the plan.
Of course, this isn't the first time a "fourth carrier" has emerged. Just a few years ago, Dish Network signed long-term tower leases to build its own 5G network. To make a long story short, Dish's parent company sold most of its spectrum in 2025 and began shutting down the network. Of course, SpaceX is a far more deep-pocketed tenant and could easily afford to build a nationwide network.
SpaceX is certainly a threat to the big three wireless carriers, but the recent sell-off appears a bit overdone. After all, SpaceX would be starting with no wireless customers at all, it holds less spectrum than any of the others, and its service isn't expected to launch commercially until late 2027. And building a competitive network would be a multiyear process at a minimum.
Let's be clear. SpaceX could certainly pressure the three major wireless carriers over time, but this isn't exactly a death sentence for them either. All have existed in the past with a fourth competitor (Sprint), and pricing power hasn't changed that much since the number dropped to three.
If you're thinking about buying tower owners as a momentum play or telecoms at a discount, it might be a smart idea to be patient. For one thing, although Crown Castle was specifically mentioned as a company SpaceX was in talks with, there isn't a signed contract or any official management acknowledgment yet. And the telecom sell-off may be overdone, as all that is happening right now is that a potential competitor (who would be starting from scratch) is negotiating with landlords.
In a nutshell, the market is pricing in a deal that hasn't happened yet, and the reaction on both the tower owner and wireless carrier side may be a bit overdone. I'm keeping an eye on some of the stocks involved, but I'm waiting for further official developments before making any moves.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft says its AI tool outperforms generalist doctors in complex diagnoses
articles.title_zh: Microsoft says its AI tool outperforms generalist doctors in complex diagnoses
articles.content_orig:
Apollon Wealth Management CIO Eric Sterner discusses how technology is driving gains in the healthcare sector on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
Microsoft researchers said in a study that a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool that can diagnose patients step by step, as a doctor would, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases.
The study, published Thursday in Science , said the AI model takes a different approach to diagnosing medical issues than most other models that seek to address those issues.
Microsoft said the AI model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient and the exams and tests that should be ordered using an "orchestrator" that organizes how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, the report said.
By contrast, existing AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient's symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
MICROSOFT PRESIDENT SAYS AI FACES FEWER SAFETY RULES THAN MILK IN CALL FOR GLOBAL REGULATION
Microsoft's research showed the AI orchestrator was more effective in diagnosing complex cases at a lower cost. (Nvidia)
While the orchestrator coordinates the steps to reach a diagnosis , the AI model first decides what questions to ask about the patient's medical history and identifies significant findings in the physical exam.
Based on what it learns from that process, it decides which tests to order, considers the results and orders further testing as appropriate. While those tasks are ongoing, the AI model is updating its working hypotheses and plans.
MICROSOFT UNVEILS CODE OF CONDUCT FOR AI MODELS AS SAFETY CONCERNS MOUNT
Microsoft will next test the AI model and orchestrator in an emergency room setting. (Philips)
The tool also outperformed human physicians when it was presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions. Researchers said assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple choice questions.
"AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those," said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, which is developing the new technology. "But, of course, that's not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary."
The researchers tasked the model with diagnosing over 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas and found that the model using the diagnostic orchestrator was over twice as accurate at "working up" the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
ANTHROPIC SILENT ON WHETHER IT WILL DISTRIBUTE SHARES TO AMERICANS FOLLOWING MUSK SPACEX PLEDGE
Researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
"We're not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We're also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up," said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
The Microsoft research team's next test will occur through a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, where it will evaluate the tool's ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms.

articles.title_orig: Coming Home to China's Future
articles.title_zh: Coming Home to China's Future
articles.content_orig:
11-13 May 2027 | Rotterdam
19-20 October 2027 | Houston
18-19 November 2026 | Singapore
By Liesl Krog China’s project cargo market is booming and Tina Yi, managing director of SAL China, is at the heart of it. She discusses the value of regional business expertise and why returning to China two decades was “the best decision ever.” From Issue 4, 2026 of Breakbulk Magazine (5-minute read) Tina Yi never thought a moment at an airport would change the course of her life. In 2006, she arrived home from the UK for a visit and found her parents waiting for her. She was working for a British-based forwarder at the time, but seeing them made her reconsider where she wanted to build her life. “I remember looking at them and thinking they were growing older, and I was not there to help. I made the decision to move back home right then and there,” she said. As an only child, Yi wanted to be closer to her parents. She settled in Shanghai, where China’s industrial expansion was creating opportunities in shipping. Power plants, steel mills and petrochemical projects were getting built, driving demand for increasingly large and complex cargo movements. Today, as managing director of SAL and JSI Alliance in China, she regards that decision as one of her most important choices. Her reason for coming home was personal, but the timing would prove important professionally. Her path into shipping, however, began far away from China. After a first degree in marketing and economics at home, she wanted to study abroad, completing a postgraduate degree at the University of Surrey before choosing a master’s in international logistics at the University of Plymouth. China had recently joined the World Trade Organization and Yi recognized the potential for shipping and logistics to grow alongside its economy. While she had no immediate plans to return home, she saw shipping as an early indicator of changes in the global economy, where her initial interest lay. Studying the industry, however, quickly revealed how well it suited her personality. “I found that shipping was a perfect match for me. It requires knowledge of the global economy, patient analysis and hands-on work. Its complexity was also very much part of the attraction,” she said. After her master’s, she faced a choice between continuing toward a PhD or putting her knowledge into practice. A job offer from Eagle Freight in the UK gave her the opportunity to do the latter. Working first with containers and then some breakbulk cargo, she began learning how the trade she had studied operated on the ground. When she returned to China, Shanghai’s ports and international connections made it a natural place to seek work. She moved into broking breakbulk cargo and handysize tonnage as China’s industrial projects generated more work and increasingly complex shipments. “In the UK my work was mostly around importing containers from China, but now I found myself on both sides, and there were some massive projects taking place in China at the time,” she said. The Curiosity Factor Among the companies she approached for freight rates was SAL. Its quotations puzzled her. “I kept thinking how they have such small vessels, much smaller than the handysize, so why the rate?” When a chartering position became available, she applied. Asked at the interview why she wanted to join, she candidly explained that she wanted to understand why SAL’s rates were so high. She laughs as she recalls her answer, but her frankness proved no obstacle. SAL offered her the job. She joined in 2007 and soon found the explanation. SAL’s vessels were specialized for heavy cargo and project shipments. Once she understood what they could do, the rates she had questioned made sense. “Ultimately, I chose SAL and they chose me,” she said. Looking back, she believes she made the right choice at the right time. Nearly 20 years later, she leads SAL’s business in China. “Heavy-lift shipping requires knowledge that takes years to acquire, and I have chosen to build mine within a company whose fleet and services have continued to expand. Each project is different and each has its own way to deliver,” she said. “I like the challenges and complexities. I found a space that I have been able to thrive in.” The work continues to hold her interest, requiring her to keep learning as projects, equipment and customer requirements change. Through the infrastructure and industrial projects she has worked on, she has also witnessed China’s economic expansion firsthand. Reading the Market For Yi, understanding China’s project cargo market starts with the policies directing its development. “China is a policy-driven market. No market moves faster. One policy shift can create a whole new industry within a year.” The country’s five-year plans provide signals about where investment and demand are likely to emerge. Studying them helps companies identify opportunities and prepare their capabilities before projects reach the shipping stage. By the time a policy produces visible demand, she believes, the best-prepared companies will already have done their groundwork. Preparation also requires regional knowledge. China’s scale does not make it a single, uniform market. The Yangtze Delta, northern China and the south have different industries, project requirements and business cultures, all of which influence how companies operate. “You have to be able to bridge those differences. Having in-depth local knowledge is critical for success, including understanding local policies and business culture.” Competition, she said, has intensified as Chinese capabilities have grown and customers have become more sophisticated. Yi’s task includes helping the head office in Germany understand these developments, identifying local opportunities and expanding SAL’s business in the region. Geopolitical uncertainty has further complicated the market. “Supply chains are more complex, with more stakeholders than ever before. Ultimately, decisions are harder and more important than ever.” Yi remains cautiously optimistic about demand, particularly across energy and industrial projects. Offshore wind operations and maintenance, floating wind farms, green methanol and ammonia projects offer opportunities, while renewable energy development also requires investment in grid and power infrastructure. “The challenge is not whether the projects exist; it is how we deliver them faster, cleaner and in a way that works for clients, governments and communities,” she said. “That takes more than machinery. It takes trust, clarity and shared understanding.” Exports of high-end Chinese equipment are another source of demand. Chinese engineering, procurement and construction contractors are undertaking overseas projects through what she describes as a greener, more selective “Belt and Road 2.0.” Data centers and semiconductor plants are also emerging as project cargo markets. These developments have changed China’s place in the industry. Once a major importer of equipment, it has become an important source of equipment, expertise and shipping capabilities. “Perhaps China missed the great maritime age of the last century. Twenty-five years ago, China was mainly a cargo market. After twenty-five years of fast growth, it is no longer just a cargo market. It has become a resource market too,” she said. “In its own way, China is opening its own great maritime era, and we are lucky to be right here, in the middle of it.” For SAL, responding means understanding where its services are needed and maintaining relationships with customers whose requirements continue to evolve. Heavy-lift capacity is limited, and customers value the certainty of securing it. They have their own shorthand for this. “Our clients often refer to SAL as ‘Space Always Limited,’ or some say, ‘Service Always Luxury,’” she said. That kind of reputation depends on relationships, and building them requires an understanding of how business is conducted locally. Yi comp

articles.title_orig: Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning
articles.title_zh: Moderna mRNA vaccine almost halves the risk of skin cancer returning
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain

            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Severe sunburn increases the risk of developing melanoma, the most serious type of skin cancer. Credit: Olga Pankova/Getty
A personalized mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of skin cancer returning or the recipient dying by 42% when used alongside an immunotherapy drug, according to long-awaited results for what could become the first approved mRNA vaccine for cancer.
Oncologists regard a risk reduction of 10% as substantial, says Kristen Radford, an immunotherapist at Mater Research in Brisbane. A risk reduction of more than 40% “would send many researchers over the Moon”, adds Seth Cheetham, a geneticist at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia.
The personalized vaccine, called intismeran, is not designed to prevent skin cancer, or melanoma, from developing in the first place, but to stop it returning in people who have already undergone surgery to remove tumours.
Anticipation for the trial results has been building since August, when the vaccine’s developers — Merck, based in Rahway, New Jersey, and Moderna, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts — announced early positive results . Data from the phase III trial will be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on 24 October. But when data were leaked online on 22 October, the companies released the key results.
The stock price for Moderna, a pioneer in mRNA vaccine technology, had been rising since the August announcement, but dropped by around 25% after the leak. Health-care financial analyst Evan Seigerman at BMO Capital Markets in New York City told media company Forbes that such reactions in the stock market probably reflect “inflated expectation into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy”.
The intismeran trial enrolled 1,137 people with moderate to advanced melanoma across 157 centres. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either a tailor-made vaccine (intismeran) alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab — which is already used to treat melanoma — or pembrolizumab plus an inactive placebo. Trial leader Georgina Long, an oncologist at Melanoma Institute Australia in Sydney, says participants have so far been followed for around 25 months and will continue to be monitored for several years to determine whether the vaccine improves overall survival. She adds that the therapy did not result in any major harmful side effects.
Roughly 15 years ago, people with advanced melanoma typically survived for only months. Today, nearly 55% are effectively cured with targeted drugs or immunotherapies, says Long. The combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab is designed for people whose cancer could return after surgery and who do not respond to immunotherapy alone, she says.
Jessamy Tiffen, a cancer geneticist at the Centenary Institute in Sydney, says that the trial results are exciting, but that only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years. “Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them,” she says. Furthermore, some people did not respond to the vaccine, she says.
Long says that her team will conduct a statistical analysis to identify who is most likely to benefit from the treatment.
To develop intismeran, Long and her colleagues sequenced DNA from a sample of each participant’s tumour to identify mutations in the cancer cells. These mutations can give rise to proteins called neoantigens, which help to distinguish cancer cells from healthy ones.

articles.title_orig: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
articles.title_zh: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
articles.content_orig:
After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’
Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.
“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.
The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.
AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.
“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.
While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.
Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.
However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.
Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun .
After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.
“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.
after newsletter promotion
In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.
“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.
In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

articles.title_orig: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
articles.title_zh: In hunt for Starlink alternative, Ukraine partners with Nokia and satellite maker ICEYE
articles.content_orig:
After SpaceX restricted use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite internet services in Ukraine, causing fast-moving drones to disconnect and drop out of the sky, Kyiv is looking for alternatives.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said on Thursday that it has signed a letter of intent to develop new defense and satellite communication capabilities in partnership with Finnish tech companies Nokia and ICEYE, which makes satellites.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement . "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."
Zelenskyy also announced a partnership with Norway this week to jointly develop air defense and communications systems that could serve as an alternative to Starshield.
Chad Anderson, founder and CEO of venture capital firm Space Capital, said such an alternative could be "two to three years away" and that "matching Starlink's scale is a longer road."
SpaceX has around around 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan McDowell .
Anderson said Starshield may be an even tougher service to replace. "The Pentagon's own contracting documents say SpaceX is the only provider that can meet some of its needs through 2026. Capital isn't the constraint any more. Launch is."
Even Starlink competitors have relied on SpaceX launches to put their satellites in orbit.
As of Friday, Ukraine officials said the country is still experiencing restrictions on Starlink, which cut connectivity for drones or other aircraft traveling at speeds over 100 mph.
Both the Trump administration and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have shirked responsibility for the unannounced Starlink service changes that Ukraine reported more than a week ago. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he would call on Musk to lift the restrictions.
SpaceX executives didn't respond to a request for comment.
Lawmakers in the U.S. from both parties are calling for a formal probe of Musk and SpaceX regarding the alleged unilateral changes the company made to its services in Ukraine.
Jay Shambaugh, a senior fellow at Brookings and professor of economics and international affairs at George Washington University, told CNBC in an email that the sudden Starlink changes are "part of a pattern since Trump came back into office of the United States acting as an unreliable ally."
Shambaugh cautioned that, "over time, that can reduce U.S. exports to the EU if those countries don't want to be dependent on something where the U.S. can cut them off."
Rivals to Starlink are on the horizon, including Amazon's Leo , France's Eutelsat and a forthcoming service from Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin called TeraWave , which has yet to deploy its first satellites.
Beyond Ukraine, several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS² , a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but its first launches aren't expected until 2029.
Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, venture and private equity investors have poured about $8 billion into Starlink and Starshield alternatives, according to research by Anderson, whose firm tracks industry deals. About $3.9 billion of that funding has gone to potential Starlink competitors, mostly Spacesail and China SatNet.
Virginia Burger, senior defense policy analyst with the Project on Government Oversight, told CNBC in an interview that the problem today is there's no drop-in replacement for Starlink, and combat is moving more into "unmanned systems, drone warfare and other systems that require high-speed internet."
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

With the Fitbit Edge announcement, Google Health previewed improved automatic activity tracking, and it’s now beginning to roll out with version 5.11 of the app.
This expanded activity tracking means the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 go from detecting 10 activities to more than 100, including:
The Fitbit Edge will also benefit from this upgrade. Google Health pairs your workout routines, historical data, manual edits, and location (permission required) with contextual reasoning.
Workouts that result in a sustained elevated heart rate and meet the minimum duration threshold are automatically logged, with a summary notification sent to the app “typically within 30 minutes.” When you “confirm or edit an activity” and log missing ones, Google will learn your patterns to tune future predictions.
Google says the end result is “nearly 2x more accurate detections,” while reducing “missed workouts by more than half.”
Expanded activity detection is appearing with Google Health 5.11, which is widely available on iOS and still rolling out on Android . After updating, users are seeing an “Expanded activity detection, built to learn” screen.

articles.title_orig: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.title_zh: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.content_orig:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
J ack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.
Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”
For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.
According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month , according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.
For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”
Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.
The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15% , according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”
On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver . “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”
In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.
At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics . Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.
Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ’em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”
Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘ What is going on?’” Price says. Generally speaking, he says, “the fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”
T wenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.
Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, or slamming on the brakes when sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was in India this week
The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.
So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?
The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions â or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.
Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.
It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.
The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.
With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.
And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.
The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now.
Rubio (left) held talks with foreign minister S Jaishankar (right) in Mumbai
Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties.
The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic.
"Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital.
"This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai."
The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works.
But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip.
Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms".
Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website.
It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets.
During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani.
The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products.
Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil.
"They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters.
Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East.
Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer.
Rubio's visit to the Jamnagar refinery was closed to the media, with images released afterwards by the Reliance Group
Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil.
India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude.
In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties.
India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority.
Then  earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
In that context, experts say Rubio's Jamnagar visit is aligned to three goals that the US appears to be pursuing: reducing India's dependence on Russian crude, encouraging greater imports of Venezuelan and American oil, and advancing a trade deal in which energy cooperation could become a key area of agreement.
There is also another possible business angle behind this push.
Kugelman says Rubio had two reasons to meet the Ambani family. First, to secure greater refining of Venezuelan oil and second to seek assurances that Reliance remained interested in backing a proposed Texas refinery.
In March, Trump announced a proposed refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas on his Truth Social platform. He said that it would be the first major new refinery in the US in 50 years.
Reliance has not publicly commented on it and there are no details on the project or when the work is expected to begin.
"The Texas facility may not be as immediately important to US interests as the arrangement tied to Venezuelan oil, but I still think it's part of the story," he says.
Trump hopes to bring down gas prices as the US heads to midterms next month
However, analysts point out that closer cooperation with Reliance and progress on energy security do not necessarily mean a trade deal is imminent.
"I don't think anyone really expected a trade deal to be announced at this point, but this trip seems to have helped get the relationship back on track, to the extent that it can, given the significant points of tension that remain," Kugelman said.
Rajani Sinha, the chief economist at credit rating agency CareEdge, told the BBC that greater cooperation could allay energy security concerns in both countries, help push the stalled trade negotiations forward and "boost trade and sentiment" in India.
Meera Shankar says that India is possibly "waiting for the US to formalise its tariff positions so that we know whether Delhi has a preferential trade deal".
She adds that, although ties between the two countries have been strained in recent times, their bilateral trade continues to grow.

articles.title_orig: Russia, Ukraine agree to ceasefire in Ukrainian city hit by food crisis, brokered by Melania Trump
articles.title_zh: Russia, Ukraine agree to ceasefire in Ukrainian city hit by food crisis, brokered by Melania Trump
articles.content_orig:
U.S. first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which will begin on October 29, the White House said on Friday.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," a White House statement said.
The development comes as Melania Trump's husband, President Donald Trump, pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reach an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," Melania Trump said in the statement.
The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from both countries to visit residents in their homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed media organization accompanying the teams to document the process, the first lady said.
Newsmax, a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted "exclusive access to document the effort."
Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people — primarily elderly residents, along with about 50 children — down from roughly 24,000 before the war, the White House said. About 90% of the city was flooded following the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House.
The statement said Melania Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.

articles.title_orig: Mitsubishi Power's $490 million Chatham County expansion to create 220 jobs
articles.title_zh: Mitsubishi Power's $490 million Chatham County expansion to create 220 jobs
articles.content_orig:
Above video: Your Friday headlines
Mitsubishi Power Americas plans to invest $490 million to expand its manufacturing operation in Chatham County, adding more than 220 jobs and nearly doubling the facility’s footprint, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced Friday.
The company will add 450,000 square feet to its Savannah Machinery Works facility at 1000 Pine Meadow Drive near Pooler. The plant, visible to drivers traveling along Interstate 16, manufactures and assembles gas turbines used to generate electricity for homes and businesses.
Mitsubishi Power said the expanded facility is expected to begin operating in early 2029.
“The expansion includes a 450,000-square-foot increase in our footprint here at the site, an additional 220 new jobs for the region and advancements in manufacturing technology and overall capacity,” said Brandon Bodie, vice president of Savannah Machinery Works.
The company expects to hire workers for positions in manufacturing, engineering, quality control, maintenance, logistics, operations and heavy machinery.
Local leaders said they hope to fill the temporary construction jobs and permanent positions with people who already live in the region.
Hugh “Trip” Tollison, president and CEO of the Savannah Economic Development Authority, said the project’s economic impact will begin before the expansion opens.
“When you think about a half-billion dollars going into one construction project, think about the labor that’s going to be needed to build the building and the concrete that’s going to be poured,” Tollison said.
He called the expansion a major win for Chatham County and said it was a highly competitive project.
“This is the largest investment to date on behalf of Mitsubishi Power Americas and will create meaningful new job opportunities for our community,” Tollison said.
Mitsubishi Power said it is expanding to keep pace with rising demand for electricity and power-generation equipment.
The company provides equipment and services for the energy industry, including gas, steam and aero-derivative turbines, geothermal systems and environmental controls. It also develops artificial intelligence technology designed to support autonomous power plant operations.
Bill Newsom, president and CEO of Mitsubishi Power Americas, said the expansion will strengthen domestic manufacturing while giving employees access to more advanced technology.
“This expansion strengthens American manufacturing and gives our people the advanced capabilities they need as they continue to deliver for our customers,” Newsom said.
Bodie said the company is also focused on developing a skilled local workforce.
“We’re excited about building a really strong workforce here that’s skilled and can support manufacturing in this community,” he said.
Mitsubishi Power has operated in Chatham County since 2009, when it established the Savannah Machinery Works operation during the Great Recession.
The expansion follows meetings Kemp and other state officials held with Mitsubishi Power and its parent company, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, in Tokyo.
“We are excited that the Savannah Machinery Works is expanding to turn those possibilities into reality,” Kemp said in a statement.
Georgia Economic Development Commissioner Pat Wilson said the state’s ports, railroads, highways and airports helped make the area attractive for the project. He also credited Georgia’s longstanding relationship with Mitsubishi Power.
“As demand for Mitsubishi Power’s products grows, this expansion is a reminder that economic development is about more than winning a project,” Wilson said. “It is about showing up, building relationships and being a long-term partner.”
The Georgia Department of Economic Development coordinated the project with the Savannah Economic Development Authority, Georgia Power and Georgia Quick Start.
Additional details about the construction and hiring schedules were not immediately available.
