articles.title_orig: Crackgate? iPhone Duo Owners Report Screens Breaking Along the Hinge
articles.title_zh: Crackgate? iPhone Duo Owners Report Screens Breaking Along the Hinge
articles.content_orig:
Some iPhone Duos are already experiencing hinge issues that cause display cracks, based on photos shared on Reddit and the MacRumors forums . Almost all of the display faults are right along the hinge, and most result in a line of bright pixels across one side of the screen.
An iPhone Duo owner in Australia said his device cracked after being opened fewer than 20 times, and there was no visible damage beforehand.
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times. I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge. There were no marks or damage on the inner screen's surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user visited an Apple Store , and Apple replaced the broken device right away. Apple is likely collecting defective iPhone Duos to research points of failure, and that research could lead to manufacturing improvements to reduce future issues.
There are several images of broken displays from demo devices in China , where the ‌iPhone Duo‌ launched hours ahead of the U.S. The backstory for most of the images is unknown, and it's possible user damage is a factor. Some reviewers who got an ‌iPhone Duo‌ early subjected it to folding tests and didn't experience screen issues, but that's a small sample.
With so many people getting iPhone Duos today, some failures are expected. It isn't known how widespread the issue is or whether we'll see an uptick in complaints over time. Hinge failures from normal use should be covered under the one-year warranty, and customers receiving an ‌iPhone Duo‌ today will also have two weeks to make a return.

articles.title_orig: Bloom Energy Stock Sinks Despite Record Revenue and a Stellar Outlook. Is It Time to Buy?
articles.title_zh: Bloom Energy Stock Sinks Despite Record Revenue and a Stellar Outlook. Is It Time to Buy?
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) delivered another blowout quarter, smashing estimates and growing profits faster than sales. Yet, its stock plunged after earnings and was down more than 12% as of Friday noon.
The company sells solid-oxide fuel cell servers that turn natural gas into electricity right at a customer's site. Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers desperately need that because the existing grid needs years to build additional capacity.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Bloom Energy can bypass the grid and swiftly deliver clean, reliable, 24/7 power to hyperscalers and data center operators. It delivered a complete fuel-cell system to Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) in 55 days last year. The tech giant was so impressed that it expanded its partnership for up to 2.8 gigawatts (GW) earlier this year.
So, what is happening with Bloom Energy stock? Why is it dropping like a rock – down 30% in one month, as of this writing?
Image source: Getty Images.
Revenue soared 138% year over year to a record $1.2 billion in the third quarter. Product sales, the fuel cell systems Bloom Energy ships to customers, topped $1 billion in sales in a single quarter for the first time.
Profit grew even faster. Adjusted operating margin jumped to 23.1% from 8.9% as revenue more than doubled while operating expenses rose only 26%. CFO Simon Edwards added that operating income in this single quarter surpassed what Bloom earned in all of 2025.
Then management raised its full-year revenue outlook for the third time this year. It now expects 2026 revenue of $4.5 billion, or about 122% growth.
Here's the kicker: Earlier in the year, Bloom Energy was guiding for a "humble" 60% revenue growth for the year. It has more than doubled its trajectory in just a couple of quarters.
So what's hurting the stock? The only metric I could find that may have miffed investors is cash burn. Bloom Energy posted negative free cash flow of $181 million in Q3.
Should investors worry? Hardly, because context is everything.
Demand is exploding, so Bloom Energy spent $153 million last quarter to scale up capacity as fast as possible. Data centers are built in phases, and Bloom is ready with its servers at each phase so operators don't have to wait.
That speed is everything for data centers.
Any data center would go after that. At a recent conference, Nvidia 's (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang explained how a 1 GW facility costs $50 billion, and just a three-month delay in building that one center could mean $10 billion in lost revenue.
Whether it's a 150-kilowatt system for a retail store or a massive 1 GW deployment, Bloom Energy has the capacity. That's precisely why global asset management giant Brookfield Asset Management (NYSE:BAM) recently expanded its financing deal with Bloom Energy from $5 billion to an eye-popping $25 billion.
Management says backlog is growing even faster than revenue. Do the math: we already know by now how rapidly revenue is growing. I expect Bloom Energy to hit it out of the park next quarter when management discloses the backlog number and issues 2027 guidance. Because, as CEO K.R. Sridhar puts it, the company is providing "power where it is needed, when it is needed, clean and always on."

articles.title_orig: Treasury proposes major restrictions to U.S. investment in Chinese biotech sector
articles.title_zh: Treasury proposes major restrictions to U.S. investment in Chinese biotech sector
articles.content_orig:
By John Wilkerson and Damian Garde
John writes about the politics of health care, and he is the author of the twice-weekly D.C. Diagnosis newsletter . You can reach John on Signal at John_Wilkerson.07.
Damian covers the global drug industry and contributes to STAT’s industry-leading events. You can reach Damian on Signal at damiangarde.67.
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration late on Thursday proposed a rule that would severely restrict future U.S. investment in the Chinese biotech sector but still allow American drugmakers to buy the rights to medicines invented in the country.
The Treasury Department proposed the rule to implement a law, called the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, that restricts U.S. investment in industries of concern to national security. The department added biotechnology to the list of industries subject to COINS restrictions, joining the likes of semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum technology.
The proposal would prohibit U.S. companies from entering financial transactions with Chinese biotech companies or Chinese manufacturers of biotechnology-related equipment and tools, according to the research firm Veda.

articles.title_orig: Mother drowns trying to save sons during Bahamas snorkeling trip
articles.title_zh: Mother drowns trying to save sons during Bahamas snorkeling trip
articles.content_orig:
A doting mother drowned while desperately trying to rescue her two children who were swept away by a strong current while snorkeling in the Bahamas, according to a report.
The 36-year-old unidentified British woman was on a snorkeling expedition with her husband and two sons south of the island of Bimini when the tragedy occurred on Tuesday, The Tribune reported .
The children were washed up by a strong current — so the mom rushed to save them, but was swept away herself, according to the outlet.
Rescuers pulled her from the water and performed CPR at a ferry dock, but the woman died at the hospital, the spokesperson said.
Linty Stuart, the owner of L&A Water Taxi, captained the boat that saved the boys and pulled the hero mom out of the water, according to the ZNS Network .
“It happened, really really fast. I’m still in shock too,” Stuart told the station, adding that big waves made the rescue difficult.
“It’s scary. We tried … It’s sad,” added first mate Jason Saunders.
The family was reportedly visiting the tropical island from a cruise ship.
The Royal Bahamas Police Force did not immediately respond to a request for information from The Post.

articles.title_orig: AI agents are roaming around consumers' bank accounts, and banks aren't happy about it
articles.title_zh: AI agents are roaming around consumers' bank accounts, and banks aren't happy about it
articles.content_orig:
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized activity from third-party AI agents operating within their customers' online accounts, according to a new Axios report .
Some of the biggest financial institutions in the U.S. say customers have given their personal AI agents, which are unvetted by banks, access to their financial accounts.
"In a lot of cases, this is just going to be customers giving their username or password to an AI agent that the bank hasn't had a chance to vet yet, that goes against the bank's terms of service," Madison Mills, senior AI reporter for Axios, told CBS News. "In other cases, in our reporting, we did find evidence that appeared to look like agents taking actions in customer accounts that were not authorized."
Examples of agent behavior that a user never approved include the AI calling a bank with a complaint without first consulting the account holder.
"So, really a nightmare of AI agent activity for banks," Mills said.
To be sure, these agents weren't going rogue or hacking customer accounts and depleting their funds, Mills said. They were largely following user instructions without the bank's permission to transact on behalf of a human account holder.
White House AI czar David Sacks responded to the Axios report, saying in a post on X that there's a clear distinction between personal AI agents that help manage users' bank accounts and hackers deploying AI for nefarious purposes.
"There's a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks," he said. "Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf."
Sacks added, "This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks."
He believes banks should support the use of such user-authorized AI agents, but that if banks want to limit their access, they could grant AI agents "read-only" permission, meaning they could view a user's spending and other bank activity but couldn't take autonomous actions.
Under such circumstances, an agent could view your purchases and opine on whether you're spending too much money eating out, for example. But it couldn't make a purchase on your behalf or take any other action.
"Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully," he said.
Mills noted that it's an industrywide problem facing dozens of financial institutions as they race to curb AI agents' access to customer accounts.
Some banks said they're taking action to make their customers aware of the risks of sharing their credentials with AI.
"Customers should not give their username and passwords to anyone. We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers to meet customers' needs while keeping their accounts safe," a Chase spokesperson told CBS News.
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon expressed concern about AI agents taking actions in customers' accounts on the company's Oct. 13 earnings conference call.
"We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said.
Charles Schwab's CEO earlier this month said the company has been blocking unauthorized agents, according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Morgan Stanley said it had not observed any unauthorized AI agent activity across its platforms.
Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment on the matter.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping May Have His Own Reasons to Avert a China-Russia-US Summit - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping May Have His Own Reasons to Avert a China-Russia-US Summit - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin have put Xi Jinping in an unusual position by expressing interest in a trilateral summit with the Chinese leader at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen mid-November. Xi’s cautious response so far – Moscow and Washington have confirmed discussion, while Beijing has yet to commit publicly – could help Europe and Ukraine avoid the worst: major powers making decisions about the region in their absence.
The idea for a meeting came from Russia and it’s not hard to see why. Moscow’s ideal outcome would reportedly be a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, echoing the 1945 conference at which the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war order in Europe. But even much more modest results would count as a success. Simply taking part in such a summit would elevate Russia’s status alongside the U.S. and China, help break its diplomatic isolation, potentially drive a further wedge between the U.S. and Europe, and provide an important platform for its narrative of Western threats to Russia.
A three-way meeting would play to Trump’s self-regard as a dealmaker and peacemaker – and quite possibly his appetite for economic gain. The United States recently eased sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports, with an initial shipment of 40,000 tonnes reportedly on its way to the U.S. Moscow has also offered to increase fertilizer exports amid shortages caused by the Middle East crisis. But Trump may also have a larger strategic motivation. He has said that nuclear disarmament , not Ukraine, should be at the top of the agenda.
With the APEC summit in China being discussed as the venue, Xi would surely welcome the huge symbolic win of being seen as the world leader capable of hosting such an important gathering – while possibly helping to widen the divide between the U.S. and Europe. But Xi also has very good reasons to avoid such a meeting. China has benefited from dealing with Washington and Moscow separately, and it has in the past insisted that both Russia and Ukraine must be involved in any peace process. A China-Russia-U.S. summit to discuss Ukraine’s future without Kyiv would undermine both those positions.
A high-profile trilateral could overshadow the APEC summit, which Beijing wants to use to showcase its economic leadership and promote openness, innovation, and cooperation . A highly publicized gathering of three major powers also would sit uneasily with Beijing’s repeated calls for inclusive multilateralism, particularly at a forum intended to promote regional economic cooperation.
A successful trilateral might make the risk worthwhile. But such an outcome is uncertain – not least because of the unpredictability of Trump and Putin. The meeting could end up dominating APEC at the expense of Beijing’s economic agenda, without producing any significant outcomes.
Lastly, while Putin and Trump have major strategic incentives to meet, Xi has a strategic reason to avoid doing so. Trump’s insistence on putting nuclear arms reduction at the top of the agenda is problematic for China. Beijing has long emphasized that its nuclear arsenal is far smaller than those of the United States and Russia – and that Washington and Moscow must make substantial reductions before China joins any talks. Abandoning this position would risk China being bound by the same rules as Russia and the U.S., despite the gap in nuclear capabilities.
But Xi may recognize that he cannot dismiss the idea of a meeting altogether. Chinese diplomats have reportedly indicated that they would not rule out a trilateral. If Xi cannot prevent such a meeting, he could at least use his position as host to shape it – a less prominent, more informal encounter with a loose agenda focused on major power relations or the global economy, rather than a formal summit focused on Ukraine or nuclear arms control that would raise public expectations. Xi could even cast himself as the host of a Trump-Putin meeting rather than a participant in three-way talks.
Such stage-management would not protect Europe and Ukraine from the United States, Russia, and China talking about them behind their backs. But it would allow European governments to frame such a meeting as nothing more than an exchange of views. A formal summit explicitly devoted to Ukraine, by contrast, would risk signaling to the world that the three leaders are entitled – by right or by force – to make strategic decisions about Europe in Europe’s absence. That alone would send a terrible precedent for the continent.
Much can still happen until the APEC summit next month. Another round of U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi are reportedly under discussion, while Trump’s views on Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy continue to shift. But whatever summitry emerges in Shenzhen, European governments must continue to insist on Ukrainian participation in any talks about the country’s future. Apart from pressing Washington to take them into account, Kyiv and European capitals should also appeal to Xi’s own reservations about a trilateral summit that also carries many risks for Beijing.

articles.title_orig: After Millions in Stolen SNAP Benefits, Trump Administration Moves to Fight Theft
articles.title_zh: After Millions in Stolen SNAP Benefits, Trump Administration Moves to Fight Theft
articles.content_orig:
ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes
            corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.
How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths
How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes
SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors
The Trump administration this week announced an overhaul of the nation’s food stamp payment system, aimed at modernizing benefit cards to protect families from electronic theft. The move comes a week after ProPublica published an investigation showing how $470 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits were stolen from recipients last year alone, in large part because these cards are technologically outdated.
ProPublica’s story highlighted victims’ experiences and examined repeated failures by Congress and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to upgrade Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards nationally. ProPublica’s reporting was shared around the department, according to two USDA officials.
The new proposed rule , officially issued by the USDA’s Food and Nutrition Administration on Friday, has been in the works since 2023 — but it was continually delayed until now. Reasons included understaffing at the USDA, especially in the wake of the Department of Government Efficiency’s cuts last year, and a backlog of other regulations that the White House budget office had prioritized. White House and USDA officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the sudden shift.
The rule will mandate that all 50 states transition from EBT cards with just a magnetic stripe on the back — which are easy for criminals to skim data from — to ones with digital microchips, which credit and debit cards have had for more than a decade, and tap-to-pay technology. Other changes include creating new federal “SNAP EBT Operating Standards” to be revised on an ongoing basis, so that the feds and states together can do a better job of keeping up with best practices in the credit card industry and the changing tactics of fraudsters.
A handful of states have already transitioned to chip cards on their own, including California, where the theft of SNAP and other public benefits was reduced by 83% in two years after the technology was adopted. But more than 40 states haven’t added chips, and hundreds of thousands of lower-income Americans continue to show up at grocery store checkout lines only to find that their food assistance for the month has been drained by thieves. NPR and other news outlets have also recently reported on this crisis.
Members of the public, including state SNAP administrators and grocery store owners who may have logistical questions about how to overhaul their EBT systems, now have 60 days to submit comments on the new USDA regulation; these will be reviewed by agency officials before the rule is formally enacted. After that, states will have two years to switch to chip cards, although their ability to meet that deadline will depend on several factors. For one, many are budget-strapped right now , due in large part to the fact that President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act slashed states’ funding for administering their SNAP programs — dollars that they could have used to upgrade their EBT systems and print and mail out the new cards.
Multiple current and former FNA officials, as well as state program administrators, told ProPublica that they are worried the agency is mandating expensive changes for states but that Congress so far has shown little sign it will provide federal funding for the chip card transition. As ProPublica reported last week, the Senate’s version of this year’s Farm Bill includes money for this purpose, but the House version does not; Democrats and Republicans remain at loggerheads about overall SNAP spending, and it is unclear what will happen. The estimated total federal and state cost of the changes is $283 million , as compared with the more than $600 million in SNAP and other benefits that are stolen from existing cards every year.
Still, the mandate that all states implement chip EBT cards “is a big deal for low-income households,” said Justin King, a longtime safety net advocate who is now the policy director for Propel , a company that helps SNAP recipients access their benefit information. He added that he was “legit surprised” by the administration’s decision.
“Theft rings don’t care about state lines. You’re just squeezing a balloon if you update one state at a time,” King said of the prospect of individual states continuing to gradually adopt chip cards without a federal requirement. “A national standard means there’s nowhere left to go” for the criminals, he said.
For the moment, at least, there are signs that the Trump administration’s posture toward this issue has shifted more broadly. On Wednesday, while barnstorming in Ohio for Republican candidates, Vice President JD Vance (whose roles include serving as the administration’s “fraud czar”) called a press conference and made a point of emphasizing that low-income families are often the victims of SNAP fraud.
This was at odds with how Vance has portrayed the problem in the past. “There are people who have Lamborghinis who currently receive SNAP benefits,” he has previously said , in a typical comment. For ProPublica’s previous article, research reporter Gabriel Sandoval reviewed dozens of speeches, social media posts and press accounts of statements made by Vance and other Trump officials, and found that they have consistently portrayed SNAP recipients as the perpetrators of fraud.
Vance also took a startlingly different tone this week toward the food stamp program itself. In his 2016 memoir “Hillbilly Elegy,” which first propelled him to fame, he wrote that SNAP recipients in Kentucky and Ohio “live off of government largesse”; he said that people in that part of the country are largely “hardworking, except of course for the many food stamp recipients who show little interest in honest work.”
But this week from the stage in southern Ohio, he said, “Step back for a minute and realize that the [SNAP] program is one of the most important social service programs that we have in the United States of America.” He went on at length: Food stamps ensure that “all of our fellow citizens, particularly children, are able to have a full belly at the end of every single night, that regardless of whether they can pay for a meal, we don’t let American children and American families go hungry. That is one of the most important and sacred things that our tax dollars go to.”
The White House and Vance’s press office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his rhetorical about-face.
Vance then had Attorney General Todd Blanche and other top officials give more details on multiple recent SNAP theft prosecutions. These included several ongoing EBT card skimming cases in Oregon in which criminal groups had allegedly pilfered the SNAP account numbers and PINs of legitimate beneficiaries and then used that data to buy bulk quantities of goods like energy drinks and baby formula — which the scammers resold for over $3 million. This is exactly the type of case that ProPublica reported on last week.
“The simple reality is that it is actually a very tough thing to go through a [grocery store checkout] line with kids,” Vance said. “To present that card, to expect to be able to take that food home to your family, to be able to cook it and provide a meal for your kids, and to be told that because of the theft of a fraudster, that you are being rejected. And there are hundreds of thousands of families all across our country, all across the state of Ohio who have had that experience.”
I’m a ProPublica reporter who writes about issues affecting poor and working-class people across the country.

articles.title_orig: First-of-Its-Kind Vaccine Ushers in New Hope for Cancer Patients
articles.title_zh: First-of-Its-Kind Vaccine Ushers in New Hope for Cancer Patients
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Moderna ( MRNA ) extended losses on Friday following a sharp sell-off in the previous session, as investors digested data from a late-stage trial of its personalized melanoma vaccine.
The stock closed down more than 1% a day after plunging more than 17% in its worst single-day performance since Aug. 20.
More than $17 billion in market value vanished on Thursday as details from the late-stage trial circulated ahead of the official debut . Merck ( MRK ), Moderna's partner on the vaccine, confirmed that the results came out early. The full data is set for release on Saturday at Europe's biggest cancer conference in Madrid.
The leaked figures, though not bad, initially failed to impress Wall Street, which had grown increasingly cautious on the stock in recent weeks after its blistering rally this year.
Goldman Sachs recently raised its target on the stock to $137 from $120 while maintaining a Neutral rating, well below the $200 level where shares closed on Friday.
Morgan Stanley also has a Neutral rating, with a price target of $95. Meanwhile, Citi analysts set an $80 target and a Sell rating on the stock last month, given its rapid run this year.
Wall Street is mostly neutral on the stock, with 5 Buy, 15 Hold, and 5 Sell ratings.
Shares of the biotech company rallied over the summer as it is no longer valued solely on its declining COVID-19 vaccine business but increasingly on its potential to become a major player in cancer treatment.
In August, Moderna announced positive phase 3 results for its personalized cancer vaccine, developed in partnership with Merck, helping drive a sharp rally in the stock.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: News - Who Crafted China’s Terracotta Army?
articles.title_zh: News - Who Crafted China’s Terracotta Army?
articles.content_orig:
XI’AN, CHINA— Science Alert reports that an analysis of fingerprints preserved in the clay of a sample of soldiers from the Terracotta Army suggests that men, women, and children contributed to the work of assembling the sculptures. Discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well about a mile away from the 2,200-year-old tomb of China’s Emperor Qin Shihuangdi, the Terracotta Army is made up of approximately 8,000 soldier statues bearing a wide variety of faces, hairstyles, and armor. Thirty-six warrior statues recovered from the same pit were surveyed for the study, and a total of 91 fingerprints were identified on them. Twelve of these prints were excluded because they seemed to come from individuals who left multiple prints. Of the 79 remaining fingerprints, 73 were left behind during the process of molding, shaping, and assembling the statues. Most of these prints were found on the warriors’ heads and arms. The other six fingerprints were left behind during the decorating process, and were found on nails and waistbands of the soldiers’ armor. The distances between the ridges of fingerprints can be used as clues to the age and sex of the person, and so a mathematical model was used to estimate who might have worked on these 36 statues. About 45 percent of the prints are thought to have belonged to men, 32 percent to women, and about 22 percent to children under the age of 15. The teens may have been working as apprentices, as described in Qin Dynasty records. “These findings challenge the long-held assumption that Terracotta Army production relied exclusively on adult male labor,” said Xiaoxi Li of the Emperor Qin Shihuang Mausoleum Site Museum. articles.title_orig: Trump says Burnham is 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
articles.title_zh: Trump says Burnham is 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has praised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the UK government's decision to approve production from the North Sea's Jackdaw gas field.
He said he had spoken with Burnham, telling reporters on Friday that the decision would "make the UK a very rich country".
Trump said: "The other prime minister, the previous man, Starmer. He's a very nice man, but he never got it done, and this one is getting it."
The decision had been subject to intense debate around its environment and economic impact and came after years of legal challenges.
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.
Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.
Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.
He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."
Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."
In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.
The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.
It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".
Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed.
However, Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision by not giving any regard to climate obligations - things he said "have to be considered in the round".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month, but that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision was "compatible" with legally binding climate commitments, adding:  "We remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050."
Environmental groups have criticised the Jackdaw approval. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said it was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Meanwhile, Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments".
During their Friday talks, Trump and Burnham spoke about the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between British and Israeli companies.
In September, the Argentinian government threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands, and earlier this month, it began legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields.
Burnham raised the "economic consequences of Argentina's coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the Islanders' right to develop their natural resources", Downing Street said.
The two leaders also discussed Ukraine, with the prime minister underlining the importance for Ukraine "to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", according to Number 10.
Starlink technology is a satellite system owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company which Ukraine has relied upon during the war.
In recent days, Ukraine has been recording issues with the network , according to sources within the defence ministry. This has affected the country's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.
The Downing Street statement added: "The Prime Minister recognised the work of President Trump to bring Putin to the negotiation table and the leaders agreed to work together, alongside international partners to bring an end to the bloodshed."

articles.title_orig: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
articles.title_zh: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
articles.content_orig:
Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany , represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

articles.title_orig: Smith & Nephew talks with J&J on orthopaedics deal fail over CEO role, source says
articles.title_zh: Smith & Nephew talks with J&J on orthopaedics deal fail over CEO role, source says
articles.content_orig:
While spinning out its orthopedics division into a solo player would’ve launched one of the largest operators in the sector alone, Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) was reportedly looking to give it a leg up by combining its DePuy Synthes business with Smith+Nephew (NYSE: SNN) in a multibillion-dollar merger.
But those plans stumbled before the finish line, according to a report from the Financial Times, as the two couldn’t come to terms on who would lead the new $34 billion company.
The report said anonymous sources described the talks as nearing completion and that there were agreements on the financial terms, but J&J — whose shareholders would’ve owned 50.1% of the enterprise — wanted its orthopedics head Namal Nawana to become CEO.
Nawana is no stranger to Smith+Nephew, after serving as its chief for about 18 months through late 2019. Nawana was tapped by J&J to lead DePuy Synthes in 2025, with his appointment announced the day it first put forward plans to separate the business .
Smith+Nephew, however, wanted to see its own CEO, Deepak Nath, carry the torch. According to the FT, Smith+Nephew chair Rupert Soames, who would have led the future board as well, said the point was non-negotiable.
The report said the total value of the proposed transaction could have reached $22 billion, almost double Smith+Nephew’s $12.6 billion market cap, with an announcement slated for this month before the deal fell apart several weeks ago.
Media relations at J&J and S+N couldn’t be immediately reached for comment.
Earlier this year Bloomberg said J&J was pursuing potential deals north of $20 billion , while reporting last month that it was also negotiating with Apollo Global Management to sell all or part of the unit.
But most recently, on J&J’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CFO Joseph Wolk said the company was now considering a spin as the businesses’ top choice.
“I am really proud of the team working to evaluate all separation vehicles and all options are better positioned today than when we announced our intentions with this business,” Wolk said on a Oct. 13 call with investors.
“Given the way DePuy Synthes is performing and the momentum Namal Nawana and his team are generating, we are leaning towards a spin as being the best option to create long-term value for Johnson & Johnson shareholders.”

articles.title_orig: 'There Will Always Be a Role Left for Us to Play' - In an AI-Filled World, Miyamoto Thinks the Human Touch Will Always Be Vital
articles.title_zh: 'There Will Always Be a Role Left for Us to Play' - In an AI-Filled World, Miyamoto Thinks the Human Touch Will Always Be Vital
articles.content_orig:
The legendary Shigeru Miyamoto has just received Japan’s Order of Culture award , and after accepting it, the creator of Mario and Zelda had something to say about the rise of GenAI in video game development.
Generative AI has become a hot topic in recent years, and with good reason; GenAI models are trained on copyrighted data , and several of the companies pushing the tech are currently involved in legal action. GenAI also carries an environmental burden, and many view it as a lazy replacement for human creatives .
Nintendo has largely resisted the allure of GenAI , so Miyamoto's lengthy comment on the matter, translated by VGC, makes for interesting reading.
"Our generation lived through a period of rapid computer development—a time when tools were constantly evolving, moving from typewriters to word processors," he begins.
"In the past, for instance, designers were taught in school how to create beautiful lettering for posters; possessing that skill alone was enough to be called a ‘designer.’ Alternatively, one could simply take a design that was trending abroad, give it a ‘Japanese-style’ twist, and be labelled a designer. However, as computers and technology advanced, a designer’s true individual capabilities, such as their innate sense of layout, finally came to the fore. I believe generative AI represents a similar shift."
He then discusses the difference between 'creation' and 'labour':
"When you set out to create, you first establish a broad structure, then begin the hands-on work: the tasks that follow, such as filling in gaps or refining the details. The tricky part is that this labour can actually be quite enjoyable. While the act of creation is inherently satisfying, there’s a danger: one might find satisfaction in the labour itself and mistakenly believe that a high-quality piece of work has been created. In that sense, the more AI replaces these tasks, the more it provides an opportunity to reflect on what’s really important, which I think is a positive thing."
Indeed, Miyamoto feels that lazy copy-pasting, something GenAI has certainly been accused of amplifying, fails to articulate the designer's intention, so humans will always be needed in the creative process, no matter how advanced GenAI becomes.
"Looking back at past designs, there are some that were created merely by copying and pasting," he says. "Yet, such work rarely stands the test of time; it lacks the individual’s particular design intention. Because the process relies on an individual’s intent, with the computer serving as an assistant for the labour, I believe that even as technology continues to evolve, and even if AI were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left for us to play.”

articles.title_orig: Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by report alleging her dad possessed child sexual abuse images
articles.title_zh: Meghan ‘deeply distressed’ by report alleging her dad possessed child sexual abuse images
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex , said Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by a report alleging that her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr. , possessed child sexual abuse images, adding that she was informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated over claims he kept child sexual abuse videos and images at his home in the Philippines. “The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who has in recent years had a limited and fraught relationship with her father. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.
The allegations against Markle Sr. were first reported Thursday by The Sun newspaper, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home. The Sun published a photo it said showed his son, Thomas  Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
Markle Sr., 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for  Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.
Markle Jr. told the Sun that he had reported his discovery to the FBI, as well as local Philippine authorities. NBC News has reached out to the FBI for comment, which did not immediately respond.
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Police in Cebu City, the location of Markle Sr.’s home in the Philippines, and London’s Metropolitan Police did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News.
In the rare statement Friday, Meghan said that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” she said in the statement.
Meghan said that she had been made aware of a letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018, that “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she added.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan said.
Asked by NBC News when Meghan was made aware of the letter to the Metropolitan Police, a spokesman for the couple said it was in the summer of 2018, after her wedding with Harry.
Separately, a source close to the couple told NBC News that Meghan’s decision not to speak publicly eight years ago should be understood in a particular context: “When she was made aware of these allegations in 2018 after they were reported to the police, they remained just that — allegations.”
“To have repeated them publicly at that stage would not only have potentially exposed her to civil action for making unsubstantiated claims, but she had also been advised that doing so could jeopardize any subsequent investigation,” the source added.
Markle Sr. told the Daily Mail he had not spoken to his son “for months” and said “these terrible lies are being made against me with no proof.” He added that he would “welcome an investigation” into the matter and labeled the accusations “a bunch of lies.”
His daughter, Samantha Markle, also told the Daily Mail of her brother’s allegations: “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
Markle Sr. married Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland, in 1979 and they subsequently divorced in 1987.
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.
The couple made their first joint public appearance last week visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.

articles.title_orig: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.title_zh: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.content_orig:
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.
Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”
That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.
Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.
This is what the policy says:
“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”
“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”
If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

articles.title_orig: Trump Blasts Vanity Fair Over ‘Fake News’ On Jared Kushner’s Alleged Undisclosed Foreign Bank Accounts
articles.title_zh: Trump Blasts Vanity Fair Over ‘Fake News’ On Jared Kushner’s Alleged Undisclosed Foreign Bank Accounts
articles.content_orig:
Jared Kushner threatened to sue Vanity Fair for publishing an excerpt of a forthcoming book describing how the president’s son-in-law oversaw foreign slush funds filled by the leaders of the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
In the new book Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East , author Matthew Cole revealed that Kushner oversaw roughly $2 billion in secret foreign bank accounts filled by the Saudis and Emiratis.
In a post on X Thursday, Kushner claimed the allegations were “completely insane and never happened.”
“These are outrageous fabrications being presented as investigative journalism. This is not journalism. It is a mixture of fantasy, fiction, and advocacy, written by someone who is either deeply disturbed or acting with sinister intent,” he wrote.
Kushner’s lawyer, Chad Mizelle, also hit back at the Vanity Fair article on behalf of his client—and threatened to sue the publication.
“Before publication, we sent Simon & Schuster a detailed 13-page letter responding to and categorically denying the extraordinary allegations made against my client, Jared Kushner, and challenging the total absence of supporting evidence,” Mizelle wrote on X.
“Vanity Fair has now published an excerpt amplifying these false and defamatory allegations. We have seen no credible evidence substantiating any of these claims, and we question what independent verification Vanity Fair conducted before publishing them,” he wrote. “We intend to pursue legal action against those responsible and hold them accountable.”
In the 13-page letter , another of Kushner’s lawyers, Alejandro Brito, insisted that Kushner had “no knowledge of, or involvement with, any such accounts.”
“Any allegation that Mr. Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorizations for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory,” the letter stated.
Speaking to reporters Friday, Donald Trump denied the potentially damning story about his son-in-law. “It’s a false story. It’s a false story. It’s a totally false story. It was totally an incorrect story. It was just fake news. Amazing,” Trump said .
The allegations contained in Cole’s book carry considerable legal weight. In 2017, Kushner was a government employee who worked in the White House, meaning he was required to submit both public and confidential financial forms and disclose any bank account to which he had access as a signatory or beneficiary. Kushner also failed to disclose himself as an agent of a foreign government, having been paid nearly $2 billion in total by foreign leaders. If he offered anything in return for the money, even just conversations with his father-in-law, then he would have violated U.S. bribery laws and the foreign agent statute.
The far-right Germany political party German Alternative für Deutschland, or AfD, has tried to enlist support from President Trump and his MAGA allies for over a decade.
The Guardian , citing a data leak from the AfD, reports the party has lobbied Trump going back to his election in 2016, with the party debating on how to word a congratulatory telegram. The final message included the wish that Trump’s “hopes as a person be fulfilled.”
The leaks comprise over 420,000 emails, documents, and personnel records from the AfD since 2013, though the info thins out after 2019. They were given to reporters by Distributed Denial of Secrets , a hacker activist group.
After Trump’s election, the AfD didn’t just congratulate him but asked that he support its efforts to remove the “enemy state” clause from the U.N. charter, a post–World War II vestige that allows action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory.” The clause is irrelevant today, but the AfD, alone among German political parties, sees it as an attack on German sovereignty.
AfD leaders also sought to make contact with Richard Grenell, who during Trump’s first term was ambassador to Germany, but was unsuccessful, and pursued contacts with former White House adviser Steve Bannon, according to the leaks.
The party holds hardline anti-immigration and Islamophobic views, and some of its members have displayed sympathies and connections to Nazism . The party’s leader in the Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted of using a banned slogan from the Nazi Party’s paramilitary wing in 2024. AfD is currently leading national polls with 30 percent support in Germany’s multiparty democracy, and in September, it won 43.8 percent of the vote in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where it is trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazis.
German intelligence labels the AfD as a suspected domestic extremist organization . Germany’s leading political parties refuse to govern or form any coalitions with it. That hasn’t stopped Trump and his MAGA allies from praising the group. Vice President JD Vance, as well as numerous State Department employees, have frequently met AfD politicians, including the party’s leader, Alice Weidel.
The party’s deputy leader, Beatrix von Storch, and her husband, Sven, were at Trump’s “Make America Great Again Victory Rally” just before his inauguration last year, and Storch bragged in a newsletter that she met Steve Bannon and Donald Trump Jr.
Trump celebrated the AfD’s September win in Saxony-Anhalt on Truth Social, posting , “Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night. They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!! President DJT.”
President Trump is losing young men.
Recent numbers from the Harvard Youth Poll show that confidence in Trump’s ability has cratered among men under the age of 30, with nearly 70 percent of them disapproving of his performance in his second term. That same number also disapproves of the Republican Party at large.
Seventy-four percent of men under 30 disapprove of how Trump has handled the economy, with the majority of them saying that their financial situations had either gotten worse or remained unchanged since he entered office. Furthermore, over half of young men said they’re entering midterms with the frame of mind to vote against Republicans rather than for Democrats, and 42 percent said their vote was a “vote in opposition to President Trump and his policies”—perhaps an indictment of both Trump and the Democratic establishment.
Trump’s success with young men was a key factor in his 2024 election victory against Vice President Kamala Harris. Men under 30 turned away from Democrats in droves, shifting nearly 30 points to the right since 2020. But much like the Black and Latino red wave that Republicans bragged about after that election, their ability to keep young men in their base has been fleeting. Rising costs, uncontrolled development of artificial intelligence, a lack of future security, and a general disapproval of the direction of Trump’s administration are all playing a part. Aside from the men, only 9 percent of young Americans in general think that the country is currently going in the right direction—presenting an ominous message for Trump as midterms rapidly approach.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Is Down 13% in a Week. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Is Down 13% in a Week. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave 's ( CRWV -2.46% ) stock has plunged 54% over the past 12 months, and it set a new 52-week low of $53.50 on Oct. 22. In the past week alone, it sank about 13%. Let's see why this neocloud stock fizzled out -- and if it's becoming a compelling buy at these prices.
CoreWeave was once an Ethereum miner, but it repurposed its Nvidia ( NVDA -0.59% ) GPUs to train AI models after the cryptocurrency market crashed in 2018.
Image source: Getty Images.
Today, CoreWeave operates 51 data centers that run over a quarter million Nvidia GPUs to remotely process AI tasks. That streamlined approach enables it to process advanced AI workloads roughly 35 times faster and at 80% lower cost than larger cloud platforms. Its largest customers include Meta Platforms , Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Nvidia also owns about 9% of CoreWeave, making it the company's top institutional investor.
CoreWeave went public last March. In 2025, its revenue soared 168% to $5.1 billion, and its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) rose 154% to $3.1 billion. Those explosive growth rates -- driven by the AI market 's breakneck expansion -- dazzled investors, and the stock surged from its IPO price of $40 per share to a record high of $183.58 per share on June 20, 2025.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/23/26
At its peak, CoreWeave's enterprise value hit $91.1 billion -- or 18 times the revenue it would generate in 2025. However, it struggled to maintain that premium valuation because investors were concerned about its steep losses and persistent dilution.
Even though its adjusted EBITDA was positive, it posted a net loss of $1.2 billion in 2025. That massive gap was driven by interest payments, equipment depreciation, lease and acquisition costs, and stock-based compensation, all of which were excluded from its adjusted EBITDA.
To stabilize its liquidity, CoreWeave issued more shares and convertible debt. That's why its share count has risen 28% since its IPO, and why it ended its latest quarter with $72 billion in total liabilities and a jaw-dropping debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3. Those glaring weaknesses suggested its business model wasn't sustainable yet, and the Fed's rate hike in September -- its first in three years -- made its messy balance sheet even less attractive.
By the end of the second quarter of 2026, CoreWeave's contracted revenue backlog had grown 246% year over year to $104 billion. For the full year, analysts expect its revenue and adjusted EBITDA to surge 151% to $12.9 billion, with adjusted EBITDA growing 144% to $7.6 billion. But on a GAAP basis, they expect its net loss to widen from $1.2 billion to $2.9 billion.
While CoreWeave's business is booming, it had only 1.85 GW of capacity at the end of June, compared to a contracted backlog of 4.2 GW. It expects to lease more data centers and buy more GPUs to narrow that gap next year, but that expansion will be costly.
For 2027, analysts expect its revenue to grow 106% to $26.5 billion, its adjusted EBITDA to grow 121% to $16.7 billion, and its net loss to narrow slightly to $2.8 billion. At its current enterprise value of $76.2 billion, it trades at just four times next year's sales and six times its adjusted EBITDA. Those low valuations should limit its downside potential, even if near-term concerns about rising rates and steep net losses weigh on its stock.
CoreWeave clearly has a first-mover advantage in the neocloud space ; it's firmly backed by Nvidia, and economies of scale should kick in as its business matures. I didn't love the stock when it skyrocketed after its IPO, but I think it's worth accumulating in the mid-50s -- as long as you can tune out the near-term noise and focus on its long-term growth potential.

articles.title_orig: Finland’s Puppy Livestream Provides Comfort in Troubled Times
articles.title_zh: Finland’s Puppy Livestream Provides Comfort in Troubled Times
articles.content_orig:
It’s dark outside. The news cycle is relentless. But Finland ’s national broadcaster has a solution: Adorable puppies , available any time, night or day.
Yle has been drawing millions of people to its website with “ Pentulive ” – Finnish for “Puppy Live” – a 24/7 live stream of Hilkka, a Lagotto Romagnolo dog, and her brand-new litter of puppies as they sleep, play and suckle enthusiastically.
Hilkka gave birth to the two females and four males on October 10. The webcam was switched on shortly after, and the puppies will remain in the spotlight until they leave for their new homes in December.
Given that puppies need up to 20 hours of sleep a day, the action can be limited, which may explain why “Pentulive,” now in its sixth season, has been labelled “ slow TV ” – a concept first trialed in Norway in 2009 with the Norwegian public broadcaster’s airing of a seven-hour train journey.
Nonetheless, viewers who tune in to the home of the anonymous breeder have been promised the chance to witness some of the “puppies’ milestone moments,” according to a Yle press statement: from opening their eyes to learning to walk and having their first playtime outside.
Despite Finland’s tiny population – just under 5.66 million – the “Pentulive” webpage had 6.5 million page views last year, according to Yle, and its social media channels attracted 20 million views. And based on viewing figures so far, this year’s puppies look set to outperform.
One of the world’s northernmost countries, Finland is preparing to usher in its long, dark winter. Temperatures can drop as low as -50°C (-58°F) and in parts of the country north of the Arctic Circle the sun does not rise above the horizon for weeks on end.
So it is hardly surprising that residents enjoy a cozy distraction from the bitter conditions outside.
How a 24-hour livestream of moose became a Swedish TV sensation
The puppy-cam was first launched in 2021 by Yle science reporter Pirjo Koskinen as part of a series on canine science. She told CNN in an email that the idea was, in part, “to shed light on a dog’s crucial first few weeks,” adding: “What happens at the breeder’s – much like with human children – influences the rest of the dog’s life.”
Distraction from the harsh reality of daily life is part of “Pentulive“‘s appeal, Koskinen believes. “It is all about caring, love, and nurturing – all those positive aspects of humanity that often get pushed aside by a constant stream of unpleasant news,” she said.
“‘Puppy Live’ offers comfort and relaxation amidst the rush of everyday life; it’s a wonderful escape from the human world into a ‘puppy bubble.’”
Sonja Mutanen, a doctoral researcher studying media and animals at the University of Eastern Finland, explained its particular appeal to Finns.
“For many viewers, these live streams are a much-anticipated highlight of the dark Finnish winter months,” she told CNN. “This kind of feel-good content can foster a sense of belonging and emotional well-being, which is important during late autumn and winter when people tend to stay at home more.”
Miiamaaria Kujala, adjunct professor of comparative cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki, said in an email to CNN that a live feed affects us in a completely different way from the short reels that are now commonplace on social media.
“The live stream offers something that appears to be missing from many of the modern busy lives: something real, genuine and fragile,” she said. “Pentulive is life-paced: It contains very calm periods and unexpectable action periods. As a live feed, it likely provokes more intense emotional responses from the observers … but it is also immensely calming to observe a sleeping puppy.”
It also provides a “sense of continuity as it follows the puppies growing older,” she said, adding: “They’re not just random animals, you learn to know them individually.”
Puppies are born ready to interact with people, study finds
This is the second litter for 5-year-old Hilkka, who is currently on leave from her role as a “school dog,” where she provides emotional support for pupils.
So far, the fluffballs have only been given nicknames by their breeder, but on Saturday they will be officially renamed. The viewing public will narrow down a selection of names, from which the puppies themselves will “choose” – by sitting in a circle of sealed envelopes and snuffling at the one that appeals.

articles.title_orig: The first broken iPhone Duos are here
articles.title_zh: The first broken iPhone Duos are here
articles.content_orig:
Now that the first folding iPhone has launched, we’ll find out quickly what can go wrong.
Now that the first folding iPhone has launched, we’ll find out quickly what can go wrong.
The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.
I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.
There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.

articles.title_orig: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.title_zh: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: Documents show German party’s scramble to request support after president’s 2016 election win and co-leader’s pursuit of Steve Bannon
A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.
The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote , came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8% , and now leads national polls at about 30% . In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation , and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist .
Its leader in the central Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted in 2024 of knowingly using a slogan of the SA, the Nazi party’s paramilitary wing. AfD politicians also attended a meeting with extremists at which a mass-deportation “masterplan” was discussed. Its 2025 election programme calls for lifting sanctions on Russia and repairing the Nord Stream gas pipelines programme . Nearly all of Germany’s other parties have kept a “firewall”, refusing to govern with it.
Media outlets including the Guardian have reported on the apparently friendly contacts between the party and the US state department during Trump’s second term.
The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.
Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader, Alice Weidel, and the key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.
The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.
The AfD said in a statement on Monday that a hosting provider used by the party had been attacked at the end of September and that “only a few mailboxes” had been copied. It told the news agency dpa that most of those mailboxes had not been used for years, and party sources were quoted as saying the published material appeared to be authentic.
AfD figures praised Trump ahead of his first election in 2016, with then leader Frauke Petry calling him a “refreshingly alternative proposition” in the spring of 2016. On the day after Trump won the presidency, Petry said the victory was “encouraging for Germany and for Europe” .
The hacked documents reveal that in the wake of his election, the party scrambled to send an ingratiating telegram to the new president.
Mainstream German politicians greeted Trump’s election with skepticism. On 9 November 2016, the then chancellor, Angela Merkel, offered Trump “close cooperation” only “on the basis of … values” including respect for human dignity “regardless of origin, skin colour, religion, gender, sexual orientation or political views”. The then defence minister, Ursula von der Leyen, called the result a “ huge shock ”. The next day the vice-chancellor, Sigmar Gabriel, reportedly called Trump the “forerunner of a new authoritarian and chauvinist international”, and he counted the AfD among its forces.
On 10 November, Petry emailed the party’s federal board proposing “an official and brief congratulatory telegram to the future US president”. German politics, she wrote, was “once again outdoing itself in politically unacceptable behaviour”; the AfD was “already perceived as the ones who don’t join in the majority howl of the political establishment” and, “as the only German party welcoming a new beginning in the US”, should say so officially.
Eleven of the board’s 13 members replied, all in favour. Current leader Weidel wrote “Yes:-)”. Beatrix von Storch, now deputy leader of the party’s Bundestag group, wrote: “Couldn’t be more of a yes.”
Board member Dirk Driesang added that Trump should also receive, “by post (?)”, the party’s manifesto in English.
The telegram went out on 11 November under Petry’s name, “on behalf of the federal board”, and was released to the press. It told the president-elect: “We are confident that you will readjust the transatlantic relationship and end the wars in Syria and Ukraine by mutual agreement with Russia.”
A second message, for the inauguration, was planned more carefully, and included a concrete request for a political favor. On 11 January 2017, Driesang asked for it to be put on the agenda of the board’s next conference call, “this time faster and better prepared”, and proposed adding a request: “Please support us in our efforts to remove the enemy-state clause from the UN charter.”
The “enemy state” clauses were written into the UN charter in 1945, and exempted action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory” from the charter’s normal rules, so that the wartime allies could move against any “renewal of aggressive policy” by Germany, Japan or their allies. The general assembly declared them obsolete in 1995 and resolved to repeal them, but the text has never been amended, because changing the charter needs ratification by two-thirds of member states and all five permanent members of the security council.
No German party currently defends the clauses, but the Bundestag’s own research service wrote in 2017 that international lawyers unanimously regard the clauses as having no practical relevance . On the German right, however, the clauses are totemic , and viewed as a limitation on German sovereignty. The AfD’s Bundestag group demanded its deletion in a 2020 motion that called it a “relic of the past” which “indirectly designates Germany an ‘enemy state’”, and every other party voted it down .
AfD’s federal board adopted the enemy state request on its call of 16 January, according to the federal office’s record of the decision contained in the leaked documents.
When the office circulated an English draft on 19 January, Georg Pazderski, then the party’s Berlin leader and a member of its federal board, objected to the tone and to the request for support: “You don’t address the president as Mr Trump, he is Mr President. Otherwise a bit wordy and flowery. I stand by it: the enemy-state clause doesn’t belong in this letter at all. You don’t do that in a letter of congratulation. It looks like a begging letter.”
Driesang replied at 6.16 the next morning: “Personally I of course find the style appropriate, otherwise I wouldn’t have written it that way.”
The office also wanted to know how the telegram should reach Trump: “directly to Trump’s campaign team … or through official diplomatic channels (e.g. the US embassy in Berlin)?”
André Poggenburg, then the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, answered: “all available channels.”
The text released on the afternoon of 20 January, signed by Petry and her then co-leader Jörg Meuthen, kept the request. It told Trump that the clause stood in Germany’s way “as a strange anachronism”, and asked him to see the AfD “as natural allies at your side, because we are the only German party in clear opposition to the wrong pol
